routes.name: Via Appia, Rome to Brundisium
citations: Strabo, Geography, trans. H. C. Hamilton and W. Falconer (London: Bohn, 1854-1857) [public domain], book 6.3.7
Lorenzo Quilici, Via Appia (Rome: Fratelli Palombi, 1989)
routes.notes: Begun in 312 BCE by Appius Claudius; extended to Brundisium. Strabo describes the road. Line through Tarracina, Capua, Beneventum, Venusia and Tarentum.
routes.goods_source: general history; not from a cargo manifest
routes.citation: Strabo, Geography, trans. H. C. Hamilton and W. Falconer (London: Bohn, 1854-1857) [public domain], book 6.3.7
routes.history: The Via Appia is named after the censor Appius Claudius Caecus, who began its first section in 312 BCE as a military road south from Rome during the Samnite Wars. It was later extended to Brundisium (Brindisi), the port for Greece and the east, and the Romans called it the regina viarum, the queen of the long roads.
routes.story: Armies, officials and, from Augustus, the couriers of the cursus publicus used the Appia. Most of the people walking it were ordinary travellers going between Rome and the port at Brundisium, where ships left for Greece.

facts.Use: military, official post, travellers and trade

routes.name: Via Egnatia, Dyrrachium to Byzantium
citations: Strabo, Geography, trans. H. C. Hamilton and W. Falconer (London: Bohn, 1854-1857) [public domain], book 7.7.4 (quoting Polybius)
routes.notes: Built from about 146 BCE across the Balkans; Strabo gives its length from Polybius. Used into Byzantine and Ottoman times.
routes.goods_source: general history; not from a cargo manifest
routes.citation: Strabo, Geography, trans. H. C. Hamilton and W. Falconer (London: Bohn, 1854-1857) [public domain], book 7.7.4 (quoting Polybius)
routes.history: The Via Egnatia was built in the 2nd century BCE, ordered by Gnaeus Egnatius, proconsul of Macedonia, according to milestone inscriptions. It ran about 1,120 km from Dyrrachium (Durrës) on the Adriatic, over the mountains past Lake Ohrid and across Macedonia and Thrace to Byzantium. Together with the Via Appia and a sea crossing, it linked Rome to the East.
routes.story: Travellers crossed from Brundisium to Dyrrachium by ship, then walked or rode the Egnatia east. Roman armies of the civil wars marched along it, and later the road carried Byzantine and Ottoman traffic toward Constantinople.

facts.Built: 2nd century BCE (Gnaeus Egnatius; exact date uncertain)
